item.research_question: How can the stability of austenite in Fe-Mn-Al duplex lightweight steels be optimized to achieve a combination of high tensile strength and high ductility without the steady flow behavior (plastic instability) observed in previous (TRIP+TWIP) steels?
item.material_system: Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al (modified) and Fe-0.3C-8.5Mn-5.6Al (previous) duplex lightweight steels; annealed variants A850, A900, A950
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting; homogenization at 1200 °C for 1 hour; hot-rolling between 1100 °C and 900 °C; furnace cooling from 650 °C; cold rolling to 1 mm; annealing at 850, 900, or 950 °C for 5 min; cooling to 400 °C at -14 °C s⁻¹ followed by air cooling
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ using ASTM E 8/E 8 M standard specimens (gage length 25 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 1 mm)
key_findings: The modified Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al steel annealed at 900 °C (A900) achieved a tensile strength of 874 MPa and elongation of 72%.
The A850 steel (annealed at 850 °C) exhibited an elongation of 95% with a tensile strength of 785 MPa.
The A900 steel showed the highest true tensile strength of 1496 MPa among the annealed variants.
The A950 steel (annealed at 950 °C) showed an abrupt reduction in elongation to about 25% despite a tensile strength of 840 MPa.
In the A900 steel, the volume fraction of martensite increased by 30% from Stage B to failure, compared to 15% in the A850 steel.
Plastic instability did not occur in the A900 steel until failure because the strain hardening rate remained considerably higher than the true stress.
The austenite fraction in the modified steel was 56% after 66%-cold-rolling and annealing at 900 °C for 30 min.
The austenite grain size in the A900 steel was 2.1 μm, compared to 1.7 μm in A850 and 2.6 μm in A950.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that decreasing austenite stability (indirectly via increased austenite fraction and alloying partitioning) promotes a dominant TRIP mechanism over TWIP in the A900 steel. This active TRIP, occurring at lower critical strains with higher rates, generates a high strain hardening rate that delays plastic instability. In contrast, the A850 steel retains high stability leading to simultaneous TRIP and TWIP, which maximizes ductility (95%) but results in steady flow behavior (plastic instability) after initial hardening. The A950 steel has too low stability, causing rapid transformation and early failure.
item.limitations: The authors state that the A850 steel, despite its 95% elongation, still exhibits steady flow behavior (plastic instability) which is a drawback for structural applications requiring high strain hardening. Additionally, the A950 steel suffers from seriously reduced elongation due to a transformation rate that is too high.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the A900 steel, with its outstanding tensile properties and reduced density, gives a promise for automotive applications as highly-deformable high-strength sheets and structural reinforcement components requiring high stiffness.
quotes: The present work gives a promise for structural applications requiring both reduced specific weight and remarkable deformability.
In the A900 steel, the high TRIP rate in the Stage B as well as the increased strain hardening rate (Fig. 3(b)) is observed.

Since the A900 steel shows outstanding tensile properties as well as reduced density, they give a promise for automotive applications to highly-deformable high-strength sheets and structural reinforcement components requiring high stiffness.
